## Problem

Manual review of AH-0MV268RXJ007M7A9 (Bot steering model to consume live ShipConfig thruster values) reported: "When I click Watch Demo (or run a capture) the AI bot behaves totally differently to when I am watching it in the gym scene. The gym scene is correct."

Investigation verified the model layer is shared and identical between the demo and the tuning gym:
- Both scenes build the brain via createCompetentBotBrain({ tunables: toCompetentOverrides(getCurrentBotTuningConfig().values) }) (PlayScene._applyBotTuning / GymBotTuning._applyTuning).
- Both scenes build the snapshot via buildBotSnapshot carrying the live Player.getThrusterConfig(); diagnostic confirmed byte-identical thruster configs in both.
- The demo seam responds to a custom ShipConfig end-to-end (new tests in src/scenes/demoMode.integration.test.ts).

The remaining 'totally different' behaviour is scenario-driven, not model-driven:
- The shipped demo (PlayScene) plays the live campaign: random offscreen asteroids (asteroidSpawnerEnabled=true), timed waves (getWaveState active → enemyWavePressurePort), lane traffic, harvesters, ghosts, boss encounters.
- The bot-tuning gym (GymBotTuning via generateRandomLevel) generates enemy-formation-only levels: the sequencer candidate pool filters out asteroid/harvester/grunt; there is no asteroid spawner, no timed waves and no boss.

## Goal

Make the bot-tuning gym exercise the same scenario pressures the shipped demo does — asteroids (with drift), timed waves, and optionally boss — so tuning in the gym transfers to the demo, and the demo does not behave 'totally differently' from the gym purely because of scenario content.

## Acceptance Criteria

- GymBotTuning (or the GymLevel base) can spawn drifting asteroids the same way PlayScene does (or reuse the shared spawn-planning helper), so the bot's hazard/asteroid responses are exercised.
- The gym scenarios include timed waves (or an equivalent wave-pressure signal) so enemyWavePressurePort decisions are covered.
- Demo↔gym observation: with the same bot tuning, the demo bot and gym bot make the same decisions given equivalent snapshots (no further divergence beyond scenario randomness).
- Full test suite passes; gym↔game parity guard (CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts) remains green.

## Out of scope
- Any further change to the bot's decision model (already delivered by AH-0MV268RXJ007M7A9).
- Changing the shipped game's demo scenario.

- **AH-0MV6MFDYG001E6PL** – Watch Demo and video recording should fly the saved bot-tuning configuration (completed)
- **AH-0MUX495VG0014MIY** – Demo mode engine: input seam and lifecycle in PlayScene (completed)

# Compile an action video

Compile a promo video package — a short promo, a longer showreel and highlight clips — from captured gameplay, selecting exciting moments from recorded on-screen action-intensity peaks, guaranteeing weapons/pickups/enemies coverage, and compiling the cuts with ffmpeg at full game-native 960×540 resolution.

## Problem statement

Captured gameplay videos and per-run **on-screen action intensity** records (`.action.jsonl`) already exist, but no promo material has been assembled from them. The project needs a compelling promo video package that shows a wide range of gameplay features — weapons, pickups, enemies — at an attention-grabbing pace, produced reproducibly from the existing capture pipeline.

## Users

- **Primary — the maintainer / release owner.** Wants showcase material (promo, showreel, individual highlight clips) to demonstrate the game's variety and pace without manual screen recording or hand-editing.
- **Secondary — prospective players / viewers.** The audience of the promo: they should see dense, exciting action within seconds (hook) and a representative spread of gameplay features.

**User stories:**

- As the maintainer, I can run one command that compiles my captured footage into a short promo, a long showreel and highlight clips, so I can share the game attractively.
- As the maintainer, I can trust that the exciting moments are chosen from recorded action-intensity peaks, so the edits feature real on-screen action rather than idle segments.
- As the maintainer, I can see which features (weapons, pickups, enemies) each clip shows, so the promo covers the whole game.

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC1 — Deliverables at full game-native resolution.** The work produces, written under the gitignored `capture-output/` tree: (a) a single compiled promo WebM of ~45–60 s, (b) a longer showreel WebM (>2 min), and (c) several short highlight clips — all WebM (VP9+Opus or VP8 fallback) at the game's **full native 960×540 resolution** (the game renders natively at 960×540: `src/core/constants.ts`), each carrying the game's own SFX audio track.
- **AC2 — Automated action-intensity peak selection.** The editing source pool and edit points are driven by the recorded per-run action-intensity series: peak windows (`burstiness ≥ 0.15` and/or `intensity ≥ 0.7`, merged within a 1.0 s gap, with lead/tail padding) as implemented by the existing pure helper (`src/scenes/core/actionIntensityHighlights.ts`) and the highlight recipe in `docs/dev/action-intensity.md` §7.5. Each selected segment is verifiable: a selection manifest lists source WebM, `.action.jsonl`, mapped video timestamps, and the intensity values that motivated the pick.
- **AC3 — Feature coverage (editorial pass).** The compiled promo and showreel visibly demonstrate a **wide range of gameplay features — weapons, pickups, enemies** (a boss segment if footage is available). A **coverage manifest** accompanies the deliverables listing, per feature, which clip and timestamp ranges show it; all three feature categories are represented.
- **AC4 — Attention-grabbing pace.** The promo opens with action (no dead air in the first ~5 s) and cuts on peaks — verified by measured criteria: the promo's sampled non-black frame ratio stays high and its average recorded intensity is at or above the documented reference band, with the per-clip intensities printed in the manifest. Editing judgment (cut cadence, ordering) is specified in the compile script's editorial config so pace is intentional and reproducible, not accidental.
- **AC5 — Reproducible, committed compile pipeline.** A committed editor script (e.g. `scripts/compile-promo.mjs` + an `npm run compile:promo` script) drives the compilation **deterministically via ffmpeg** (installed on the host, per producer decision): trim, reorder, join and mux the source clips without hand-editing. The script (`--help`) documents inputs/outputs and prerequisites, fails with clear errors when ffmpeg or source footage is missing, and its pure parts (manifest/selection logic) are unit-tested hermetically.
- **AC6 — Testing/validation.** The pure selection/planning logic of the compile script has hermetic unit tests; the delivered video files are validated (decodable, non-trivial non-black pixels, audio track present, correct resolution) by a validation step in the pipeline.
- **AC7 — Documentation updated to reflect the changes**, including the compile pipeline, prerequisites (ffmpeg), command examples, manifest formats, and any relevant references in `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md` / `docs/dev/action-intensity.md`.
- **AC8 — Full project test suite must pass** with the new changes.

## Constraints

- **Game-native resolution only (960×540)** — no 1080p upscale; the game has no native 1080p detail (producer decision Q4=A).
- **ffmpeg as the joining tool** — a host-level dependency (not currently installed); the pipeline must document and detect it. No other new system dependencies (producer decision Q5=B).
- **`capture-output/` is gitignored** — deliverables themselves are never committed; only scripts, tests, docs and (small) manifests are committed.
- **Independent of multi-scene capture tooling** — do not block on *Scripted Gameplay Videos (AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC)*; record it as related work only (producer decision Q3=A). Fade-transition re-filming is a possible future improvement, not a requirement here.
- **No manual screen recording / hand-editing** — everything flows from the existing capture pipeline outputs (`npm run capture`, `--all-scenarios`, demo runs) and recorded action-intensity series.
- Repo conventions apply: never edit `.pi/`, `skill/`, `command/` or agent-infrastructure dirs; work item referenced in commits; UK English.

## Existing state

- `npm run capture` — headless-Playwright gameplay video capture: 960×540 WebM (VP9+Opus), 60 fps, with the game's own SFX (proven 2026-10-06). Flags: `--duration`, `--tail`, `--count`, `--all-scenarios`, `--scenario <name>`, `--list-scenarios`, `--scripted`, `--headed`, `--max-duration`.
- Action-intensity metric implemented and recorded per run as `<run-id>.action.jsonl` (per-tick `rawScore`/`intensity`/`smoothed`/`burstiness`) — *Implement on-screen action intensity metric (AH-0MUZMTTYH008KVS2)*, done.
- Time→video join helper (`capture_started` marker + `mapTimeToVideo`) and pure highlight window selection — `src/scenes/core/actionIntensityHighlights.ts` (+ tests), *Capture: video join + highlight selection (AH-0MUZQG13S006KL8K)*, done.
- Sample footage already in `capture-output/` (demo runs + `boss-four-hits` scenario clip).
- No ffmpeg on the host; no video-joining npm dependency.
- No promotion/compile tooling exists yet.

## Desired change

1. **Gather source footage** covering weapons, pickups and enemies at full native resolution (new `npm run capture -- --all-scenarios` and demo/full-run clips as needed).
2. **Automated highlight plan** — a script reads each source run's `.action.jsonl`, computes peak windows (reusing the documented highlight recipe), and produces an ordered edit plan (clip + in/out points) sized to the promo/showreel/clip target lengths.
3. **Editorial pass** — an editorial config guarantees feature variety (weapons, pickups, enemies each represented) and an attention-grabbing order: open on action, jump-cut across peaks, brief context shots where pacing benefits.
4. **Compile with ffmpeg** — a committed driver (`npm run compile:promo`) trims, orders, concats and muxes (audio preserved) into the three deliverables + manifests, validating outputs.
5. **Document & test** — docs for the pipeline and its prerequisites; hermetic unit tests for the pure plan/selection logic.

## Key Files (predicted)

- `scripts/compile-promo.mjs` (new) — ffmpeg-driven compile orchestrator: edit-plan generation, ffmpeg invocation, output validation
- `scripts/compile-promo.test.ts` (new) — hermetic tests for the pure edit-plan/selection logic (no ffmpeg, no browser)
- `scripts/compile-promo.d.mts` (new) — type declarations (repo convention for `.mjs` scripts)
- `package.json` — `compile:promo` script entry
- `src/scenes/core/actionIntensityHighlights.ts` — reference only: highlight thresholds/recipe to reuse (port the pure logic into the script where the TS helper is dev-gated/not importable from Node)
- `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md` and/or `docs/dev/action-intensity.md` — § pipeline documentation, ffmpeg prerequisite, manifest formats
- `capture-output/` — deliverables + manifests (gitignored, never committed)

## Related work

- *Compile an action video (this item, AH-0MV9DB68T002IROX)* — top-level promo assembly.
- *Scripted Gameplay Videos (AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC)* — related (not a blocker): future multi-scene capture with 0.25 s fades could replace cross-scene cuts; record as `related-to`.
- *Implement on-screen action intensity metric (AH-0MUZMTTYH008KVS2)* — done; provides the `.action.jsonl` series.
- *Capture: video join + highlight selection (AH-0MUZQG13S006KLK8)* — done; provides the highlight recipe and time mapping.
- *Spike: automated gameplay video capture (AH-0MUWMFF3C002WOBK)* — done; the capture pipeline producing source footage.
- `docs/dev/action-intensity.md` §7.5 — highlight recipe (peak thresholds, gap merge, lead/tail).
- *Screen action intensity tracking and analysis (AH-0MUZCSJXQ004TREN)* — done; research/decision behind the action-intensity metric (find-related).
- *SettingsScene: key-binding remapping + reset to defaults (AH-0MUA8BGE0006UAU4)* — completed, tangential (find-related).
- *Test matrix and shared fixtures for the collector-drone path (AH-0MVBMPYPB004RP0P)* — open, tangential (find-related).

## Risks & assumptions

- **ffmpeg availability (risk/mitigation):** host lacks ffmpeg; pipeline must detect its absence and fail with a clear installation message; document `apt`/`brew`/static-binary install in the docs. CI/other hosts need the same prerequisite — noted as an assumption that the operator's build hosts can install it, else this becomes a blocker to raise.
- **Native resolution ceiling (assumption):** "full resolution" = game-native 960×540; any 1080p/social-platform requirements are out of scope (follow-up item if ever needed).
- **Highlight pool quality (risk):** automated peaks may pick repetitive or visually similar moments; the editorial config + coverage manifest are the mitigation (variety, dedupe by feature, manual overrides allowed in the edit plan).
- **Scope creep (risk):** multi-scene fades (AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC), 1080p output, audio editing, or a social-platform pipeline are explicitly **out of scope**; if discovered during implementation, record as new linked work items (`discovered-from:AH-0MV9DB68T002IROX`) rather than expanding this item.
- **Existing capture format assumption:** source footage is WebM (VP9+Opus) 960×540 as produced by `npm run capture`; ffmpeg trims/concat/muxes against that container (Opus audio preserved).

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q1 (Map, to producer): "Deliverable shape — (A) one compiled ~45–60 s WebM at 960×540 like existing captures / (B) longer showreel >2 min / (C) several short highlight clips?" — **ANSWERED: "All of the above but at full resolution."** Interpretation: produce all three deliverables (promo, showreel, highlight clips) at full game-native resolution — resolution clarified in Q4. Source: interactive reply.
- Q2 (Map, to producer): "How should exciting segments be chosen and ordered? (A) fully automatic peaks / (B) automated peaks + editorial pass for variety and pace / (C) fully manual." — **ANSWERED: B** — automated peak selection as source pool plus an editorial pass guaranteeing weapons/pickups/enemies coverage and attention-grabbing pacing. Source: interactive reply.
- Q3 (Map, to producer): "Relationship to multi-scene capture tooling (AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC)? (A) independent / (B) dependent, wait for fades / (C) defer until tooling lands." — **ANSWERED: A** — independent; compile from existing single-scene captures; multi-scene tooling recorded as related work only. Source: interactive reply.
- Q4 (Map, to producer, round 2): "The game renders natively at 960×540 — what does 'full resolution' mean? (A) game-native 960×540 / (B) 1080p upscale (needs ffmpeg or a game-resolution change)." — **ANSWERED: A** — game-native full resolution (960×540); no 1080p upscale. Source: interactive reply.
- Q5 (Map, to producer, round 2): "No ffmpeg on the host; how should clips be joined? (A) browser-based edit console re-recording via captureStream / (B) install ffmpeg, drive from a Node script / (C) defer to multi-scene tooling." — **ANSWERED: B** — install ffmpeg on the host and drive it from a committed Node script. Source: interactive reply.

Research summary: the capture pipeline (`npm run capture`) and the action-intensity series (`.action.jsonl`) are complete and sample footage already exists in `capture-output/`; the pure highlight recipe lives in `src/scenes/core/actionIntensityHighlights.ts` and `docs/dev/action-intensity.md` §7.5. The game's native resolution is fixed at 960×540 (`src/core/constants.ts`), and ffmpeg is not installed on the host (`which ffmpeg` — none), which the operator resolved by choosing to install it.

## Plan: decomposition

Decomposed into 9 child work items covering all 8 acceptance criteria (100 % AC
coverage verified by the `tree_coverage` review). Test-first ordering: the
hermetic test suite (AH-0MVDV47VO0081VUK) is created before the pure
implementation (AH-0MVDV4OKN001OT18), and the full-suite verification
(AH-0MVDV560Z002PSLT) depends on every implementation/doc child.

| # | Child | ACs covered | Depends on |
|---|-------|-------------|-----------|
| 1 | Capture: export action-intensity series + join anchor (AH-0MVDV4DMY001Z7CU) | prerequisite for AC2 | — |
| 2 | Tests: pure compile-promo edit-plan and selection (AH-0MVDV47VO0081VUK) | AC6 (test-first) | — |
| 3 | Implement: pure edit-plan and selection logic (AH-0MVDV4OKN001OT18) | AC2 | 1, 2 |
| 4 | Editorial config and feature-coverage manifest (AH-0MVDV4RJ300459ZF) | AC3, AC4 | 3 |
| 5 | ffmpeg compile driver and output validation (AH-0MVDV4PNZ004ZWOZ) | AC5, AC6 | 1, 3, 4 |
| 6 | Gather source footage covering weapons/pickups/enemies (AH-0MVDV4SYG008X8TY) | AC3 (source pool) | 1 |
| 7 | Produce and validate promo/showreel/highlight clips (AH-0MVDV50Z20071RF4) | AC1 | 5, 6 |
| 8 | Documentation for the promo compile pipeline (AH-0MVDV53RA0079F8N) | AC7 | 5, 7 |
| 9 | Full project test suite passes (AH-0MVDV560Z002PSLT) | AC8 | 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 |

Vertical-slice note: child 1 is a capture→disk slice (series + anchor);
children 2–4 are a pure logic slice (tests → selection → editorial);
child 5 is the ffmpeg slice; child 7 is the end-to-end runtime slice
(pool → deliverable + manifests + measured pace); child 8 is the docs slice.

### Plan: changelog

- **2026-10-18** — Initial decomposition by the `plan` skill:
  - Created 9 children (see table) and wired 16 dependency edges.
  - Ran the six automated review stages and the AC-coverage review
    (100 %, `proceed`).
  - Recorded the discovered capture-side series/anchor export gap (see
    Appendix P1) and created child 1 to close it.
  - Effort/risk re-estimated by the `effort_and_risk` skill.

## Appendix: planning questions & answers

The five producer decisions Q1–Q5 recorded in the intake Appendix above remain
the authoritative answers; they were re-read (not re-asked) during planning.

- **P1 — DISCOVERY, 2026-10-18 (Map, planning session).** Repository
  investigation found that the parent's "Existing state" claim that
  per-run `<run-id>.action.jsonl` records already exist is **not yet true**:
  no `.action.jsonl` files exist in `capture-output/`, and the pure serialiser
  `src/scenes/core/actionIntensitySerialiser.ts` has **no production caller**
  (only its unit test). `scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs` writes only the WebM;
  telemetry (with `state.actionIntensity`) is held in the page's JSONL sink
  (`localStorage` key `ai_hell_telemetry_jsonl`). The §7.5 join inputs
  (`capture_started` epoch ms from `buildCaptureStartedMarker`, and the
  telemetry run-header `startedAt`) are produced in memory but not persisted
  next to the WebM.
  - **Resolution (assumption, documented for review):** close the gap by
    wiring `npm run capture` to persist `capture-output/<run-id>.action.jsonl`
    plus a join-anchor sidecar, reusing the **already-documented** §7.3 format
    and the existing pure serialiser — child *Capture: export
    action-intensity series + join anchor (AH-0MVDV4DMY001Z7CU)*. This is the
    minimal path mandated by AC2 (which requires a `.action.jsonl` per run)
    and invents no new format. Evidence: `ls capture-output/*.action.jsonl`
    (none), `git log -S serialiseActionIntensitySeries` (serialiser commit
    only), `grep -rn serialiseActionIntensitySeries src/ scripts/` (no
    production caller).
  - **OPEN QUESTION (to producer, non-blocking):** if you would prefer the
    compiler to instead derive the series from a `npm run record`
    telemetry dump (rather than having `npm run capture` write it), say so and
    child 1 will be re-scoped. Recommendation: keep the capture-side export
    (it matches docs §7.3 and keeps WebM + series co-located).
- **P2 — ASSUMPTION (Map, planning session).** The parent AC4 "documented
  reference band" for average recorded intensity is **not yet documented**
  anywhere in `docs/dev/`. Planned resolution: child 7 documents the band
  (with its calibration basis) and child 8 records it in the docs; the band is
  derived from the captured peak windows rather than fixed a priori.
  - **OPEN QUESTION (to producer, non-blocking):** do you want a specific
    minimum mean-intensity threshold (e.g. ≥ 0.4) written into the docs, or is
    a calibration-derived band recorded from the produced footage acceptable?
    Recommendation: calibration-derived band, documented with the measured
    values.
- **P3 — DECISION (Map, planning session).** Approval gate check returned
  `request_approval: false` (effort Medium, risk Medium — not Extra Large +
  High/Severe), so the plan proceeded without a producer approval pause, per
  the plan skill's gate rule.

# Audio Design Chapter — retro-arcade survival game GDD

## Problem statement

The GDD currently defines only SFX (§7.3 Audio Direction) and states background music is out of MVP scope with no musical direction defined. The game lacks a documented musical identity (scales, motifs, harmonic language, instrumentation, dynamic mixing, and state-driven music architecture) to guide composition and implementation when music is eventually built.

## Users

- **Audio designers and composers** — need a definitive musical language (scales/modes, motifs, progressions, instrumentation palette) to write consistent, on-brief music.
- **Technical audio programmers** — need the implementation contract (bus architecture, priority tiers, ducking, state machine, middleware guidance) to build or integrate the music system.
- **Game designers / producers** — need per-game-state emotional targets and transition rules to keep audio aligned with gameplay pacing.

User stories:

- As an audio designer, I want documented scales and motifs per game state, so my compositions match the game's emotional arc without guesswork.
- As a technical audio programmer, I want the music state machine and dynamic-mixing rules defined, so I can implement or configure the music engine against a fixed contract.
- As a producer, I want music explicitly scoped as design reference (out of MVP), so the shipped SFX scope (§7.3) is not disturbed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — New chapter file created:** An **AI Hell Music System** chapter is saved as a Markdown GDD addendum at `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md`. Its **musical substance** is taken from the producer's original *Music & Thematic Audio Design* brief (Phrygian Dominant + Lydian scales; Combat Motifs A and B and the ambient "Star Drift" motif; the combat, boss and ambient progressions; the FM 2–4 operator + chiptune implementation notes — reproduced under **Source material (A)** below) and laid out in the **8-section + 2-appendix** professional structure of the approved reference brief (Ross, v1.0, 16 October 2026): **1** Audio Vision Statement; **2** Musical Identity (2.1 Tonal Language, 2.2 Core Motifs, 2.3 Chord Progressions); **3** Instrumentation Palette; **4** Dynamic Mixing Rules; **5** State-Driven Music Transitions (5.1 Transition Design Principles, 5.2 Transition Matrix, 5.3 Stinger System); **6** Implementation Guidelines (6.1 Audio Middleware, 6.2 Music Event Architecture, 6.3 Parameter Mapping Table, 6.4 Technical Specifications, 6.5 Audio Budget Table); **7** Composer and Sound Designer Briefs (7.1 Composer Brief, 7.2 Sound Designer Brief); **8** Audio Accessibility; **Appendix A** Motif Reference Sheet; **Appendix B** Glossary. The reference brief is a **structure exemplar only** — its Tableau card-game substance (D Dorian, harpsichord/cello ensemble, card-table SFX, parlour ambience) must **not** be imported into AI Hell's chapter.
- [ ] **AC2 — GDD §7.3 references the chapter:** The "Background Music" subsection in GDD §7.3 (Audio Direction) is updated to link the new chapter file, while retaining the explicit statement that background music is **out of MVP scope** (design reference only; SFX remains the only in-scope audio).
- [ ] **AC3 — GDD §8 future-scope row updated:** The "Background music" row in §8 (Future Scope) references the new chapter file so the doc stays self-consistent.
- [ ] **AC4 — Doc-only change, no behaviour impact:** No game code, SFX behaviour, or runtime audio pipeline is changed; existing §7.3 SFX scope and the shipped ToneForge pipeline remain authoritative for the MVP.
- [ ] **AC5 — Validation:** A new docs guard `src/audioDesignChapterDocs.test.ts` (following the sibling `*Docs.test.ts` convention, e.g. `src/powerUpWeaponRosterDocs.test.ts`) asserts, and passes, that: (i) `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` exists; (ii) it carries all 8 numbered sections plus Appendix A and Appendix B of the approved reference structure; (iii) GDD §7.3's "Background Music" subsection links the chapter **and** still states music is out of MVP scope; (iv) the GDD §8 "Background music" row links the chapter. All links resolve, and any index/table-of-contents entries are updated.
- [ ] **AC6 — Full project test suite must pass with the new changes** (docs-only; confirms no accidental code impact).

## Constraints

- Music remains **"design reference, out of MVP scope"** — no change to the existing scope stance in GDD §7.3 or §8.
- The chapter is a **synthesis**, not a verbatim import (Q4/Q5, this session): the **musical content** is the producer's original retro-arcade brief reproduced faithfully (Source material (A)); the **document structure** follows the approved reference brief (author: Ross; version 1.0; dated 16 October 2026 — Source material (B)). The reference brief's Tableau card-game substance is **not** carried over.
- Follow the repo's docs naming/style conventions where sensible (singular Markdown addendum under `docs/`, referenced by relative link).
- UK English throughout.

## Existing state

- GDD §7.3 "Audio Direction" covers MVP SFX: baked ToneForge WAV pipeline, SFX event catalogue, per-enemy/per-player audio character, beat-synced explosion accents, and a one-paragraph "Background Music" subsection stating music is a nice-to-have, out of MVP.
- GDD §8 "Future Scope" lists "Background music — Synthwave / retro electronic soundtrack" with no further detail.
- No existing work item implements or specifies background music; the work log contains no musical-identity design doc.

## Desired change

- Add the Audio Design Chapter (AI Hell musical content in the approved reference structure) as a standalone GDD addendum document.
- Point GDD §7.3's "Background Music" subsection and §8's future-scope row at the new document.
- Keep all gameplay/SFX/runtime behaviour untouched.

**Key Files:**
- `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` (new) — the Audio Design Chapter addendum (confirm filename at implementation)
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — §7.3 "Background Music" subsection updated with a link + scope note; §8 "Background music" row updated with a link
- `src/audioDesignChapterDocs.test.ts` (new) — docs guard following the sibling `*Docs.test.ts` convention
- `./README.md` (if it indexes docs) — optional link to the new chapter

## Related work

- **Update GDD audio design section and code comments (AH-0MTGS9DZ6001IFJR)** — completed; historical GDD §7.3 SFX additions, unrelated to music direction.
- **Update audio documentation (AH-0MUTYV9QV0000HDT)** — completed; ToneForge baked-asset pipeline docs; source of the current §7.3 scope language.
- **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)** — this item.
- See also GDD §7.3 and §8, and `docs/AUDIO_TONEFORGE_CUE_MAPPING.md` for the authoritative SFX cue catalogue.

## Risks & assumptions

- **Scope-stance divergence (medium):** the chapter is "APPROVED FOR PRODUCTION" in tone while the GDD keeps music out of MVP. Mitigated by AC2/AC3 explicitly framing the chapter as design reference; implementation remains a future work item.
- **Middleware references (FMOD/Wwise) are forward-looking:** the game currently uses Phaser/Web Audio with baked assets (§7.3). The chapter's §9 middleware guidance is design intent for future integration, not an instruction to adopt FMOD/Wwise in the MVP. Noted in the chapter context if needed.
- **Content divergence from shipped SFX:** the chapter (§6.4) proposes procedural SFX recipes that differ from the shipped baked-ToneForge SFX catalogue. The chapter is an addendum; §7.3 remains authoritative for MVP SFX (per constraint). Recorded as an assumption.
- **Scope creep:** producer may later want chapter sections mapped into the live audio system — that is future implementation work, tracked separately, not part of this docs-only item.

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Where in the GDD should the 'Music & Thematic Audio Design' content live? Music & Thematic Audio Design

This section defines the musical identity of the game, focusing on scales, motifs, harmonic language, and usage guidelines across gameplay states. The goal is to merge retro‑arcade space tension (Asteroids) with relentless survival energy (Vampire Survivors), using a coherent musical palette that supports procedural layering and dynamic intensity shifts.

🎼 1. Core Musical Identity

The soundtrack is built around two complementary scales:

Primary Combat Scale — Phrygian Dominant

Used for: wave combat, boss spawns, high‑intensity survival phases.

Scale Formula: 1 ♭2 3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7Example (E): E – F – G♯ – A – B – C – D

Why:

Retro‑arcade tension

Exotic, driving, instantly “space danger”

Works extremely well with FM bass, square leads, and arpeggiators

Provides strong melodic hooks with minimal notes

Secondary Ambient Scale — Lydian

Used for: menus, starfield travel, upgrade screens, low‑intensity exploration.

Scale Formula: 1 2 3 ♯4 5 6 7Example (C): C – D – E – F♯ – G – A – B

Why:

Bright, floating, cosmic

Contrasts the combat scale without breaking aesthetic cohesion

Ideal for pads, shimmering arps, and soft synth textures

🎵 2. Melodic Motifs

Motifs are intentionally short (2–6 notes) to support looping, procedural recombination, and chiptune‑style repetition.

Combat Motif A — “Incoming Wave”

Scale: Phrygian Dominant (E)Contour: Rising tension → abrupt dropNotes: E – F – G♯ – F – E – DUsage:

Triggered at the start of each enemy wave

Can be fragmented into E–F–G♯ for micro‑stingers

Works well as a 3‑note arpeggiated alert

Combat Motif B — “Survival Pulse”

Scale: Phrygian Dominant (E)Rhythmic Cell: Dotted + straightNotes: G♯ – A – G♯ – F – EUsage:

Mid‑combat loop

Easily reharmonized for intensity scaling

Can be doubled with FM bass for crunchy retro drive

Ambient Motif — “Star Drift”

Scale: Lydian (C)Contour: Floating, circularNotes: C – E – F♯ – E – D – CUsage:

Menu screens

Upgrade/shop interface

Slow arpeggiated background texture

🎹 3. Harmonic Progressions

Retro arcade music often avoids complex harmony, but these progressions provide structure while staying loop‑friendly.

Combat Progression (Phrygian Dominant)

E – F – E – D

Minimalist, modal, tense

Works with pulsing bass and rapid arps

Can be expanded to E – F – G♯ – F – E – D – C – D for boss phases

Boss Progression (Phrygian Dominant, extended)

E – C – D – F – E

Chromatic tension

Strong “danger escalation” feel

Supports heavy FM brass or distorted square leads

Ambient Progression (Lydian)

C – D – E – F♯

Bright, drifting, spacey

Works well with pads and slow-moving textures

Can be looped seamlessly or expanded to C – G – D – F♯

🔧 4. Implementation Notes

Motifs should be stored as atomic musical objects (interval sets + rhythm cells) for procedural recombination.

Combat layers should increase harmonic density (more voices, faster arps) rather than changing the motif.

Ambient layers should use long‑release envelopes and minimal rhythmic content.

FM synthesis (2–4 operators) and chiptune waveforms (square, triangle, noise) define the retro palette.

All motifs should be designed to loop cleanly at 1–2 bars for dynamic layering.

# Implement the Music System defined by the Audio Design Chapter

## Goal

Build the runtime background-music system for AI Hell against the fixed design contract captured in
`docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` (produced by **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)**).

User story: *As a player, I want a dynamic, retro-arcade soundtrack that responds to combat intensity, so
that runs feel like the relentless survival experience the game is aiming for; and as a developer I want the
music engine driven by a documented parameter/state contract, so behaviour is testable and reproducible.*

> **Scope stance:** this is **future scope, out of MVP** (GDD §8). The MVP ships baked ToneForge SFX only
> (GDD §7.3), and §7.3 remains authoritative for SFX. This item must **not** be started until the design
> chapter exists and has been reviewed, and it must **not** promote music into the MVP without an explicit
> producer decision.

## Background

- AI Hell currently has **no background music** by design: GDD §7.3 keeps music out of MVP scope, and the
  player-fire grid is deliberately quantised to a **silent internal 80 BPM beat** (AH-0MUAYB8EH005RJ8B).
- SFX are build-time baked WAV assets rendered deterministically by ToneForge and played through Phaser's
  shared `AudioContext` (`src/audio/effects.ts`); the authoritative cue catalogue is
  `docs/AUDIO_TONEFORGE_CUE_MAPPING.md`.
- The Audio Design Chapter specifies the musical identity (Phrygian Dominant combat scale, Lydian ambient
  scale, Combat Motifs A/B, "Star Drift"), instrumentation palette, dynamic-mixing rules, state-driven
  transitions, parameter mapping, audio budget and accessibility requirements.

## Expected behaviour and outcomes

- A music system that plays layered/stemmed music driven by an explicit game-state parameter, with
  bar-boundary transitions, stingers, and ducking, as specified by the chapter.
- Music state follows gameplay (e.g. menu/attract, wave combat, boss, low-health tension, run end) with the
  transition rules and timings given in the chapter, and never disrupts the beat grid or the SFX mix.
- Reproducible, deterministic behaviour suitable for automated tests; no audio regressions to the shipped SFX
  pipeline.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — Contract traceable to the chapter:** every implemented music state, transition, stinger and
      mixing parameter traces to a named section of `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md`, recorded in a mapping
      table in the implementation docs.
- [ ] **AC2 — Musical content matches the documented identity:** the delivered cues/stems use the chapter's
      scales, motifs and progressions (Phrygian Dominant combat, Lydian ambient, Combat Motifs A/B,
      "Star Drift"), verified by an explicit audit table (motif → scale degrees → usage state).
- [ ] **AC3 — State machine implemented and tested:** transitions occur only at the documented boundaries
      (bar boundaries unless a stinger cut-in is specified), with unit tests covering each transition in the
      chapter's transition matrix, including invalid/reset paths.
- [ ] **AC4 — Dynamic mixing implemented:** ducking, per-layer volume targets and the priority tiers behave as
      specified; SFX intelligibility is preserved (music ducks under key SFX cues) and is covered by tests.
- [ ] **AC5 — Autoplay and accessibility compliance:** no audio before a user gesture (`AudioContext`
      resume discipline, GDD §7.3); the chapter's accessibility requirements (e.g. music/SFX independent
      volume, mute, and any reduction options) are implemented and documented.
- [ ] **AC6 — Budget met:** the shipped music respects the chapter's audio budget (memory, streaming,
      polyphony, layer count) on the supported targets, measured and recorded.
- [ ] **AC7 — Docs updated:** GDD §7.3 and §8 are updated to reflect the shipped music system, and
      `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` is marked as implemented for the sections that ship.
- [ ] **AC8 — No SFX regression:** the existing ToneForge baked-SFX pipeline and cue catalogue remain
      unchanged and their tests pass; any chapter §6.4 procedural SFX recipes are explicitly **not** adopted
      unless decisioned separately.
- [ ] **AC9 — Full project build and test suite pass.**

## Constraints

- **Blocked by** the docs item **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)** — this item
  must not begin before `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` exists.
- Music stays **out of MVP scope** until a producer decision promotes it (GDD §7.3, §8).
- Keep the gameplay SVG/vector aesthetic and retro-arcade palette of the chapter; UK English in all docs.
- §7.3 (baked ToneForge SFX) remains authoritative for SFX; the chapter is an addendum whose §6.4 procedural
  SFX recipes are design reference only.
- Prefer reusing the existing audio plumbing (`src/audio/effects.ts`, shared `AudioContext`, manifest-driven
  playback) over introducing new runtime dependencies; any middleware adoption (the chapter's FMOD/Wwise
  guidance) is a separate decision — the web build currently has no middleware.

## Approach (indicative)

1. Confirm scope with the producer (MVP vs post-MVP) and record the decision on this item.
2. Ingest the chapter into an implementation mapping table (state → parameter → cue/stem set → transition).
3. Decide the delivery mechanism (baked stems via ToneForge + `AudioContext` playback, per the existing
   pipeline) versus a runtime synthesiser; record the trade-off before coding.
4. Implement the music state machine and mixing layer behind a single facade, mirroring the existing SFX
   façade style; add unit tests per transition and per mixing rule.
5. Add accessibility controls and the autoplay guard; verify budget and measure on target hardware.
6. Update GDD §7.3/§8 and the chapter's implemented-sections marker.

**Key Files:**
- `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` — the design contract (prerequisite)
- `src/audio/effects.ts` — existing SFX façade / shared `AudioContext` plumbing to reuse
- `src/scenes/core/CombatCoreScene.ts` — where combat-state music parameters would be driven from
- `src/core/rules.ts` — game-rules config (including `beatBpm`) that music tempo must stay coherent with
- `src/audio/` — new music module + tests
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — §7.3 and §8 updates

## Risks & assumptions

- **Overlap with the shipped silent beat grid (medium):** player fire is quantised to an internal 80 BPM beat.
  Music must be tempo-coherent with that grid or the two will fight; assume music tempo is either locked to
  `beatBpm` or documented as intentionally independent.
- **Chapter/SFX divergence (medium):** the chapter's §6.4 procedural SFX recipes differ from the shipped baked
  catalogue; §7.3 stays authoritative (AC8).
- **Middleware assumption (low):** the chapter's FMOD/Wwise guidance is forward-looking; no middleware exists in
  the web build, so it is design intent only.
- **Scope creep into MVP (medium):** music is out of MVP; promotion needs an explicit producer decision.

## Related work

- **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)** — prerequisite; produces the design contract.

- GDD §7.3 (SFX, authoritative for MVP), GDD §8 (Future Scope — "Background music"), and

- Beat grid / timing context: AH-0MUAYB8EH005RJ8B (beat-aligned fire grid), AH-0MV01HNLU008S5E3 (beat-timed
  explosion accents).

◆  Game Design Document  ◆

Chapter 7 — Audio Design

Version    1.0    Status    DRAFT
Date    16 October 2026    Author    Ross
Audience    Composer  •  Sound Designer  •  Audio Programmer    Location    Dublin, Ireland
◆   Table of Contents

◆Appendix A  —  Motif Reference Sheet

◆Appendix B  —  Glossary

1    Audio Vision Statement
Tableau sounds like a room that knows something you do not. The sonic world of the game is built on intimacy and implication: the close acoustics of a candlelit parlour, the murmur of conversation just beyond hearing, the creak of an old leather chair as someone leans forward to make a decisive play. Every layer of audio — from the lowest ambience hum to the highest harpsichord ornament — is calibrated to make the player feel that they are not merely playing a card game, but participating in a ritual that has been performed in this candlelit room for centuries. The aesthetic is arcane and ceremonial, yet never cold. It breathes. It whispers. It pays attention.

The musical identity is unapologetically layered and tension-forward. Borrowed from the hush of a late-night jazz club — that particular quality of suspended time between a musician's phrases — the score maintains perpetual forward momentum through rhythmic restraint rather than bombast. Baroque harpsichord ornamentation provides melodic filigree above a slow-moving, cello-led harmonic foundation, evoking old leather and ink, the scent of candlesmoke, and the particular concentration of minds engaged in high-stakes play. Silence, half-tempo breath, and strategic harmonic ambiguity are primary compositional tools. What is not played is as significant as what is.

The primary emotional arc of a Tableau session moves through four distinct experiential phases: curiosity at the outset, as the player surveys the table and assesses possibility; mounting tension through the mid-game as scores converge and options narrow; release at the climactic moment of resolution — a single card, a revealed hand, a decisive score; and finally reflection, in which the end-state music creates space for the player to sit with the outcome, win or lose. Audio must serve each phase faithfully without rushing the transitions. The score is a collaborator, not a commentator.

2    Musical Identity
2.1   Tonal Language
The tonal world of Tableau is rooted in modal harmony, chosen for its capacity to hold simultaneous qualities of darkness, sophistication, and unresolved longing — qualities that map directly onto the game's aesthetic and dramatic arc.

Primary Mode: Dorian
The Dorian mode serves as the game's default harmonic voice throughout all active gameplay states. Dorian's characteristic raised sixth degree (in D Dorian: B♮) gives it a quality that is simultaneously minor in flavour yet elevated in character — darker than a major key, but warmer and more sophisticated than pure natural minor (Aeolian). This distinction is critical: Tableau is not mournful, it is concentrated. All core chord progressions, melodic lines, and harmonic voicings in AMBIENT and ENGAGED states must remain within or clearly imply the Dorian mode centred on D.

Secondary Mode: Phrygian Dominant
The Phrygian Dominant mode (the fifth mode of the harmonic minor scale; in D: D–E♭–F#–G–A–B♭–C) is employed as a harmonic intensifier reserved for moments of arcane revelation — rare card draws, special ability triggers, and the CLIMAX mix state. Its characteristic flattened second degree (E♭ in D) creates an immediate sense of the uncanny: familiar enough to feel anchored, foreign enough to signal that the ordinary rules have shifted. Composers must treat Phrygian Dominant as a guest mode that visits and departs — it should not sustain for more than a phrase or two before resolving back to Dorian context.

Reserved Mode: Ionian (Major)
Ionian (pure major) is forbidden during gameplay. It is reserved exclusively for the victory resolution at game end. The sudden arrival of a bright, unambiguous major key — after an entire session in Dorian — should feel like sunlight breaking through clouds: earned, surprising, and emotionally legible even to players with no musical training. Even in the Resolution Motif harmonisation for victory, the transition to Ionian should be brief and clearly delineated. Any use of Ionian during active gameplay rounds will dilute this payoff and must be avoided.

◆ Key Centre Reference

Base key centre: D. All harmonic content must be conceived and notated relative to D as root. Transposition for specific instrumentation may be discussed with the composer, but all documentation and event naming in this chapter uses concert pitch in D.

2.2   Core Motifs
Tableau's score is built on three foundational motifs. These cells are the genetic material of the entire soundtrack — they should recur, transform, invert, fragment, and combine across all music states and stingers. Thematic coherence across the full audio experience depends on the composer's disciplined deployment of these motifs. Each motif is documented below with its full usage specification.

Motif I — The Tableau Motif
A four-note cell comprising the pitches D – F – G – B♭. This interval sequence (minor third, major second, minor third) outlines a D minor seventh chord without its fifth, creating an open, slightly ambiguous harmonic identity. It is the musical embodiment of the game's name: present from the first moment, recurring throughout, always slightly incomplete — like a hand of cards not yet fully revealed. As the primary theme, it functions as both a melodic statement (solo cello or harpsichord) and a counter-melody when the harmonic texture thickens in mid-game states.

Motif II — The Wager Motif
A three-note chromatic descent: C# – C♮ – B. Compact, deliberate, and harmonically destabilising — this semitone-plus-semitone descent creates the sensation of a bet being placed, a card turned face-down, a decision crossed. The Wager Motif is never harmonised: it must always appear in bare, unaccompanied monophony (or near-unison octave doubling at most). Any harmonisation would soften its edge and undermine its function as a signal of critical, unambiguous stakes. It appears on high-value card plays, bidding moments, and whenever the game engine flags a decision as decisive.

Motif III — The Resolution Motif
An ascending perfect fifth: D – A. The most harmonically stable interval in the document, and intentionally the simplest motif — after the chromatic anxieties of the Wager and the modal ambiguity of the Tableau Motif, the bare ascending fifth lands with the weight of inevitability. It appears exclusively at round-end and game-end. For a defeat or neutral ending, it may be stated plainly in Dorian context. For a victory ending, it may — and should — be harmonised in Ionian (D major), unlocking the only moment of unambiguous brightness in the entire score.

4    Dynamic Mixing Rules
Tableau employs a vertical re-mixing system: rather than transitioning between different pieces of music, the score is structured as a set of parallel stems (individual instrument tracks) that are dynamically faded in and out based on the current game state. All stems are recorded and delivered simultaneously, bar-aligned, and at matching tempo within each BPM zone. The audio engine (FMOD) reads the current GameState parameter and smoothly crossfades between stem volume configurations in real time.

This approach ensures that transitions between mix states are always musically coherent — instruments enter and exit at harmonically appropriate moments — rather than creating jarring cuts or mismatched musical phrases. The result is a score that feels continuously alive and responsive without being perceptibly mechanical.

5    State-Driven Music Transitions
5.1   Transition Design Principles
The guiding principle for all Tableau music transitions is perceptual invisibility. A player who is not actively listening for musical changes should not perceive state transitions as deliberate or mechanical. To achieve this, the following rules govern all transition behaviour throughout the audio system.

Bar-boundary synchronisation: All stem-level transitions initiate on the next musical bar boundary following the trigger event. The game engine must signal the audio middleware at the moment of trigger; the middleware queues the transition to execute at the next bar downbeat. This eliminates rhythmic dislocation.
Maximum transition window: No transition should take longer than 2 musical bars to complete (i.e., all fades in and out must reach their target volumes within 2 bars of commencement).
Crossfade-only layer changes: Stems entering and exiting must always crossfade — abrupt unmutes or mutes are forbidden except in the CLIMAX stinger cut-in (see below).
The Unaware Player Rule: Before shipping any transition, the audio programmer must test it with a non-audio team member playing naturally. If the transition is perceived as a jarring or obvious change, it must be revised.
CLIMAX Exception — Stinger Cut-In: The CLIMAX state entry is the sole exception to the bar-boundary rule. The CLIMAX stinger fires immediately on trigger via a hard cut-in (see Section 5.3), while the underlying adaptive stems continue from wherever they are in their bar cycle. The stinger is mastered to sit above the adaptive stems and momentarily dominates the mix, creating the intended sense of sudden, heightened drama.

6    Implementation Guidelines
6.1   Audio Middleware
Primary Recommendation: FMOD Studio (Firelight Technologies). FMOD is the preferred middleware solution for Tableau's adaptive audio system for the following reasons:

Event-based architecture: FMOD's event model maps cleanly onto Tableau's trigger-driven design. Each music state, stinger, and SFX can be authored as a discrete event with full parameter control.
Parameter-driven transitions: The GameState and ancillary parameters (see Section 6.3) can be driven directly from game code, enabling real-time smooth crossfades and logic-driven behaviour without requiring audio team involvement at runtime.
Seamless looping: FMOD's loop region and transition marker system allows bar-aligned loop points to be authored directly in the DAW and respected precisely at runtime — essential for Tableau's vertical remixing architecture.
Unity and Unreal integration: Full native integration packages are available for both major engines. The FMOD Unity integration in particular has a well-maintained and actively supported API.
Multi-stem event architecture: FMOD's multi-track event layout allows all stems within a music state to be authored and balanced within a single event, reducing event management complexity for the audio programmer.
Secondary Option: Audiokinetic Wwise. Wwise is an equally capable middleware solution and may be substituted if the development team has existing Wwise expertise or licensing arrangements. Wwise's RTPC (Real-Time Parameter Control) system is equivalent in capability to FMOD's parameter system, and its Music Switcher object can handle the state-based transitions described in Section 5. If Wwise is selected, the event naming conventions in Section 6.2 should be re-expressed as Wwise Switch Containers and Sound Banks, but all musical and design intent in this document remains valid regardless of middleware choice.

◆ Middleware Decision Gate

Middleware selection must be confirmed by the audio programmer in collaboration with the lead engineer before score recording commences, as stem delivery format and loop point metadata may differ slightly between FMOD and Wwise authoring workflows. This decision should be made no later than the end of pre-production.

Sample rate: 44.1 kHz
Bit depth: 24-bit WAV
Channels: Stereo (unless otherwise specified; mono stems are acceptable for solo instruments if the mono image is preferable)
Loop points must be bar-aligned: loop start and loop end must fall exactly on bar downbeats, verified in a DAW before delivery
All stems within a music state must share an identical bar count and be delivered at the same length, facilitating frame-accurate parallel playback
Pre-roll: 4 beats of silence before bar 1, retained in the file for FMOD alignment purposes
Ambience Loops
Minimum loop length: 4 minutes before perceptible repeat; 8 minutes preferred for parlour room tone
Loop crossfade baked into the file: a 2-second crossfade at the loop point to eliminate audible seam
Fireplace recording: minimum 6 minutes raw; processed to minimum 4-minute loop
Format: 44.1 kHz, 24-bit WAV; compressed to Vorbis in FMOD bank for distribution
Sound Effects (SFX)
Sample rate: 44.1 kHz
Bit depth: 16-bit
Normalised to −1 dBFS peak (do not use loudness normalisation — peak normalisation only)
Deliver all SFX variations as individual mono or stereo files as appropriate; spatialisation applied in engine
No pre-roll silence required on SFX files
Stingers
All stinger files must include a 250ms silence tail appended to the end of the audio content to prevent click artefacts on event completion in FMOD
Deliver at 44.1 kHz, 24-bit WAV
Stingers should be pre-mixed (all instruments within the stinger balanced relative to each other) but delivered as a single stereo file; no stems required for stingers
6.5   Audio Budget Table
Platform    Max Simultaneous Voices    Music Stems    Ambience Layers    SFX Polyphony    Approx. Compressed Asset Size
PC (Primary Target)    64 voices    Up to 8 simultaneous stems (full CLIMAX state)    3 layers (room tone, vinyl, fireplace)    32 concurrent SFX voices    ~180–220 MB (Vorbis Q6–Q7)
Mobile (iOS / Android)    32 voices    Up to 5 simultaneous stems; tension layer limited to col legno only on mobile (prepared piano suppressed)    2 layers (room tone + vinyl; fireplace optional, disabled by default)    16 concurrent SFX voices    ~80–100 MB (AAC / Vorbis Q4–Q5)
Web (Browser)    16 voices    Up to 4 simultaneous stems; TENSE and CLIMAX collapse to 4-stem mix (cello, harpsichord, pizzicato, one tension stem)    1 layer (room tone only; vinyl and fireplace suppressed)    8 concurrent SFX voices    ~40–55 MB (Vorbis Q3–Q4; streamed where possible)
◆ Mobile Audio Programmer Note

On mobile, the prepared piano Tension Layer stem should be replaced by a subtly increased col legno volume during TENSE and CLIMAX states to maintain dramatic differentiation within the reduced voice budget. The muted horn swell may be retained on high-end mobile devices (iPhone 14 and above; Android equivalent) as a conditional asset loaded based on device capability detection at session start.

7    Composer and Sound Designer Briefs
7.1   Composer Brief
Overview
You are composing the adaptive score for Tableau: an intimate, arcane card game set in a candlelit parlour. The score must function as both a mood-setter during the lobby and an emotionally responsive dramatic companion during gameplay. Every bar of music should feel as though it is being performed live in the next room — close, considered, and entirely present.

Deliverables
Deliverable    Specification    Notes
AMBIENT stems    16-bar loop; solo cello + harpsichord (lute stop); 68–72 BPM; D Dorian; Parlour Idle progression    Must loop seamlessly. Bar-aligned loop point. 24-bit / 44.1 kHz WAV. Deliver cello and harpsichord as separate stems.
ENGAGED stems    8-bar loop; full Core Ensemble (cello, harpsichord, pizzicato strings, brushed percussion); 80–88 BPM; Building Stakes progression    Deliver each instrument as a separate stem. Pizzicato and percussion must be rhythmically locked. Harpsichord: 8’ register.
TENSE stems    8-bar loop; Core Ensemble + col legno contrabass; 90–98 BPM; Building Stakes progression with Arcane Surge intrusions    Deliver col legno as separate stem. The transition from ENGAGED to TENSE BPM should feel like a natural forward lurch, not a mechanical shift.
CLIMAX stems    Maximum 16-bar loop; full ensemble including horn swell; 90–98 BPM; Arcane Surge progression dominant    Full orchestral texture. This is the emotional ceiling of the score. Deliver all stems separately. Horn swell: deliver as a single stem with a soft attack ramp baked in.
RESOLVE stems    8-bar loop; Core Ensemble (cello + harpsichord only); 60–68 BPM; Denouement progression    The Resolution Motif should be the first melodic statement heard on entry into RESOLVE. Deliver as a separate 4-bar one-shot file plus the looping stem.
Stingers    4 stinger files: Arcane Reveal, Danger, Comeback, Round Start. All harmonically compatible with D Dorian in all mix states. With 250ms silence tail.    Deliver as single mixed stereo files. Do not deliver stems for stingers. See Section 5.3 for instrumentation and harmonic constraints.
Menu Theme    Full 90-second version of the AMBIENT score with a defined intro (8 bars) before looping into the AMBIENT loop. The intro should feature the Tableau Motif in its complete 4-note form on solo cello.    Delivered as a standalone stereo file for use on the main menu before the adaptive system is initialised.
Reference Mood Vocabulary
The following adjectives should be active in the composer's mind at all stages of the process: intimate, candlelit, ceremonial, concentrated, layered, whispered, arcane, unhurried, tension-forward, sophisticated, fateful, ancient, alive.

Forbidden Elements
No major key (Ionian) during gameplay. Major harmony is the game's ultimate reward — deploying it earlier dilutes its impact to zero.
No electronic synthesis. This score lives entirely in the acoustic world. No synthesisers, virtual instruments, or sampled electronic textures. Live or very high-quality live-capture samples only.
No drum kit. The brushed percussion must remain archaic and intimate. Any use of a recognisable trap kit or drum machine feel is immediately inconsistent with the game's aesthetic.
No wall-to-wall orchestration. Space and silence are as compositional as any note. Avoid filling every bar with multiple simultaneous voices.
No tempo that feels rushed. Even the TENSE state at 90–98 BPM should feel concentrated and deliberate, not hurried. If in doubt, slower is correct.
7.2   Sound Designer Brief
Overview
Your task is to create the diegetic sound world of Tableau's physical environment: the cards, the tokens, the room, the fire. Every sound should feel like it was recorded in the same candlelit parlour as the music. The unifying aesthetic principle is premium physical authenticity: real materials, real acoustics, real objects. No synthetic substitutes where a real recording is achievable.

Card SFX Requirements
Source all card sounds from real, high-quality playing cards (ideally 100% plastic or high-quality linen-finish card stock). Record on a surface that approximates felt or baize — a wool surface or actual card-table baize is preferred. Record in a dry, controlled acoustic environment (treated room or padded space). Capture at minimum 96 kHz / 24-bit and down-sample to 44.1 kHz after processing to preserve transient clarity.

Deal SFX: Record 12–15 raw takes of cards sliding across baize at various speeds and weights; edit down to the 6–8 best variations. No artificial reverb — the room sound should come from the recording environment itself.
Flip SFX: Record 8–10 card flip takes; aim for variations in attack weight. Retain the natural resonance tail; do not truncate it.
Collect SFX: Record 4–6 shuffle/collect takes; post-process by blending a separately recorded harpsichord grace note (provided by the composer as a separate asset) underneath the physical card sound at approximately −12 dB relative to the card sound. This blend should be barely audible — a subliminal shimmer, not an obvious musical element.
UI Palette Constraints
All UI sounds must be derivable from acoustic instruments (harpsichord, strings) — no electronic beeps, clicks, or generated tones.
The confirm/select grace note should feel like a natural harpsichord ornament, not a UI notification sound. It must not interrupt the musical flow perceptibly.
The error/invalid sound must contain no musical pitch. If, after processing, any pitch is perceptible, the sound must be reworked. A very short, damped, hollow wooden knock or muted string thud are the target references.
Ambience Loop Specifications
Parlour Room Tone: Record in a real room: a quiet, medium-sized domestic or institutional space. Capture the room's acoustic signature including any incidental sounds (distant traffic, building settle, air movement) at a level below audibility in the final mix. Minimum 10-minute raw capture; edit to a 4-minute seamless loop.
Vinyl Crackle: Record from an actual vinyl record playing a blank locked groove, or source from a high-quality foley library (preferred: dry, unprocessed raw capture). Band-limit as specified in Section 3 instrumentation notes.
Fireplace: Capture a real wood fire in a domestic fireplace or controlled environment. Record at close range (approximately 1.5–2 metres) for a warm, intimate quality rather than a large open-hearth sound. Avoid recordings with sharp pops or crackles that would require excessive editing.
Foley Sourcing Philosophy
The Tableau SFX palette should be sourced entirely from real recorded objects wherever possible. The chip/token clink should be recorded from actual glass or crystal objects. The card sounds should come from real cards. The fireplace from a real fire. This commitment to physical authenticity is not merely aesthetic: it ensures that the sound world of the game coheres with the acoustic identity of the musical score and supports the player's suspension of disbelief that they are present in a real, physical, candlelit room.

8    Audio Accessibility
Tableau's audio design must be fully accessible to players across a wide range of hearing abilities, hardware configurations, and environmental listening contexts. The following principles and requirements govern all audio accessibility considerations.

Volume Controls
The game must expose four independent volume sliders in the settings menu, each independently controllable from 0% to 100%, with persistent save across sessions:

Slider Label    Controls    Default Level
Master Volume    Overall output level; scales all other sliders proportionally    80%
Music    All stems in music/main_adaptive and stingers; menu theme; victory fanfare and defeat sting    75%
SFX    All card, token, and UI sound events in sfx/ hierarchy    85%
Ambience    All events in ambience/ hierarchy (room tone, vinyl, fireplace)    60%
Visual Feedback Companions
Every game-critical audio cue must have a corresponding visual companion element. Audio may be absent (device muted, headphone unplugged, player is hearing-impaired) and the game must remain fully playable. The following pairings are mandatory:

Card Deal / Flip: Visual card animation (slide, flip) is the primary communicator; the SFX is a secondary reinforcement.
Danger Stinger: A visible on-screen indicator (e.g., a subtle edge vignette, score proximity warning, or indicator icon) must fire simultaneously with the Danger stinger.
Arcane Reveal Stinger: The rare card reveal animation serves as the visual companion. The stinger must never be the sole indicator of a legendary card draw.
Comeback Stinger: A visible score change animation or lead-change notification must accompany the stinger.
Victory Fanfare / Defeat Sting: Full result screen with clear victory/defeat visual state. The fanfare and sting are supplementary.
Round Start Stinger: A visible round-start UI element (round number, deal animation) is the primary signal; the stinger reinforces it.
Mix State Changes (TENSE, CLIMAX): Subtle visual UI changes — e.g., a slight warm shift in the UI colour temperature, a score tension indicator bar — must accompany escalating mix states. These visuals must be independently readable by a player with no audio.
No Audio-Only Information Principle
This is an absolute constraint: no game-critical information may be communicated exclusively through audio. Every piece of information carried by a sound must also be carried by a visual element. This applies to all states, all platforms, and all game events without exception.

Headphone vs. Speaker Mixing
The primary mix target for Tableau is stereo headphone listening: intimate, close, with a narrow stereo image appropriate to the game's intimate aesthetic. The mix should not rely on wide stereo placement or spatial separation as an information carrier. For speaker playback (monitors, mobile speaker, laptop), the mix should remain coherent and legible without stereo imaging — all critical content must be present in the centre of the stereo field. The audio programmer should implement a Mono Compatibility check as a post-processing step on all final stems and SFX before ship. No critical content should be lost or phase-cancelled in mono.

Appendix A  —  Motif Reference Sheet
Compact reference for all production team members. Refer to Section 2.2 for full motif descriptions and usage rules.

Motif Name    Pitches    Interval Content    Scale Degrees (D Dorian)    Emotional Trigger    Mix State Usage
The Tableau Motif    D – F – G – B♭    Minor 3rd + Major 2nd + Minor 3rd    1 – ♭3 – 4 – ♭7    Identity, curiosity, presence; the game's signature    AMBIENT (primary statement); ENGAGED (counter-melody); TENSE (fragmentation); forbidden in CLIMAX as a complete statement; RESOLVE (distant echo optional)
The Wager Motif    C# – C♮ – B    Minor 2nd + Minor 2nd (descending)    ♭7 (chromatic) – 6 – ♭6 — outside pure Dorian; implies Phrygian Dominant approach    Stakes, danger, irreversibility; the moment of committing    TENSE (Danger stinger); CLIMAX (contrabass doubling); forbidden in AMBIENT and RESOLVE; never harmonised in any state
The Resolution Motif    D – A    Perfect 5th (ascending)    1 – 5    Closure, inevitability, the exhale after decision; earned rest    RESOLVE only (one-shot at state entry); Victory Fanfare (harmonised in Ionian); Comeback stinger (embryonic form); forbidden in all other states
Appendix B  —  Glossary
Definitions of audio production terminology for non-audio team members. Terms are listed alphabetically.

Term    Plain-Language Definition
Bar Boundary    The exact moment when a new musical bar begins — the "downbeat." In Tableau's audio system, transitions between music states only happen at bar boundaries so that the rhythm never sounds disrupted. Think of it as waiting for the right moment in a conversation before changing the subject.
BPM (Beats Per Minute)    The speed of the music, measured as the number of rhythmic beats per minute. A BPM of 60 means one beat per second; 120 means two beats per second. Lower BPM feels slower and more contemplative; higher BPM feels more energised. Tableau ranges from 60 BPM (RESOLVE state) to 98 BPM (TENSE/CLIMAX states).
Col Legno    An Italian instruction for string players meaning "with the wood." Instead of using the hair of the bow to draw sound from the strings normally, the player hits or scrapes the strings with the wooden shaft of the bow, producing a dry, percussive, scratchy sound. Used in Tableau for the contrabass in the Tension Layer.
Cross-Fade    A technique where one audio layer gradually fades out while another simultaneously fades in, so there is never a moment of silence between them. It is the audio equivalent of a dissolve in film editing. Tableau uses crossfades for all mix state transitions to avoid jarring cuts.
Diegetic    Sounds that exist within the world of the game — sounds the characters or players could theoretically hear if they were physically present. Card shuffles, chip clinks, and fireplace crackles are all diegetic. Non-diegetic sounds are external to the game world, like background music that the players wouldn't hear. In Tableau, the distinction is blurred intentionally: the music is designed to feel as though it is also present in the room.
Dorian Mode    A type of musical scale — a specific pattern of notes from a root pitch. The Dorian mode sounds dark and sophisticated, similar to a natural minor scale but with one note raised (the sixth degree), giving it a quality that is melancholic but not despairing. In D Dorian, the notes are D, E, F, G, A, B, C. This is Tableau's primary harmonic language.
FMOD Parameter    A numeric value sent from the game code to the FMOD audio middleware that controls how music and sound behaves in real time. For example, the GameState parameter tells FMOD which mix state is currently active, and the audio system responds by adjusting which instruments are heard and at what volume. Parameters are the bridge between the game's logic and the audio's behaviour.
Harmonic Voicing    The specific arrangement of notes in a chord — which notes are played, in which octave, and in what order from low to high. Two chords can contain the same pitches but sound very different depending on their voicing. Open voicings (notes spread widely across the pitch range) sound spacious and atmospheric; close voicings (notes clustered together) sound dense and intimate. Tableau's harmonic voicings are specified as open and spacious to match the game's aesthetic.
Loop Point    The exact position in an audio file where playback jumps back to the beginning of a loop, allowing music or ambience to repeat seamlessly for an indefinite duration. In Tableau, all music stems must have their loop points precisely aligned to bar boundaries so that when the music loops, the rhythm continues without any disruption or audible glitch.
Phrygian Dominant    A specific musical mode (scale pattern) associated in Western music with mystery, the exotic, and the arcane. It is characterised by a very small interval — just a semitone — between the first and second notes of the scale, giving it an immediately unsettling and ancient quality. In Tableau it is used for special card reveals and the most intense musical moments. In D, the Phrygian Dominant scale is: D, E♭, F#, G, A, B♭, C.
Pizzicato    An Italian instruction for string players meaning "plucked." Instead of bowing the strings, the player plucks them with a finger, producing a short, bright, percussive sound rather than a sustained tone. In Tableau, pizzicato strings provide the rhythmic pulse of the score during active gameplay — a quiet, regular heartbeat beneath the melodic cello and harpsichord.
Polyphony    The number of individual sounds that a device or system can play simultaneously. A device with a polyphony of 16 can play 16 different sounds at the same time. Exceeding the polyphony limit causes the oldest or quietest sounds to be cut off to make room for new ones. Tableau's audio budget table (Section 6.5) specifies different polyphony limits for PC, mobile, and web platforms.
Stem    An individual audio track containing a single instrument or group of instruments, delivered as a separate file. A piece of music might be delivered as multiple stems — a cello stem, a harpsichord stem, a percussion stem — so that each layer can be controlled independently in the game engine. This is the foundation of Tableau's vertical remixing system: the game can fade individual stems in and out to change the emotional intensity of the music without playing a different piece of music.
Stinger    A short, pre-composed musical cue that fires as a one-shot event on top of the adaptive background music in response to a specific game event. Unlike the background score which loops continuously, a stinger plays once and ends. Stingers in Tableau are used for dramatic moments such as a rare card draw, a danger warning, or a comeback. They must be carefully composed to be harmonically compatible with all possible musical contexts they might play over.
Vertical Remixing    A technique in adaptive game audio where multiple versions of the same music are played simultaneously as separate layers (stems), and the mix changes dynamically by adjusting the volume of each layer rather than switching between different pieces of music. The musical coherence is maintained because all layers are written in the same key and tempo; the emotional intensity is controlled by deciding which layers the player hears at any given moment. This is the primary adaptive music technique used throughout Tableau.
TABLEAU  •  Audio Design Chapter  •  Version 1.0  •  Draft  •  16 October 2026
